---
title: "Backup and Restore"
execute:
  eval: false
---

A complete PPSV recovery has three independent parts:

1. the SQLite database;
2. the persistent fallback directory; and
3. the primary facility project pool.

The repository backs up the first two. The storage team must provide and test
the pool snapshot/restore policy separately. A database backup alone is not a
complete request-file recovery.

## External backup destination

`PPSV_BACKUP_DIR` is mandatory and must point to a mounted external backup
destination. Provisioning rejects a path that resolves to the VM root
filesystem unless `PPSV_ALLOW_LOCAL_BACKUP=1` is deliberately used on a test
VM. Production must not use that override.

Set `PPSV_BACKUP_EXPECTED_SOURCE` to the exact reviewed output of:

```bash
findmnt -n -o SOURCE -T "$PPSV_BACKUP_DIR"
```

Every backup and deployment verification compares the live source with that
value and stops if the mount is missing or changed. This prevents an empty local
mount point from silently receiving backups.

Record at minimum:

- mount source and target;
- storage owner and escalation contact;
- encryption and access policy;
- capacity alerting;
- retention policy;
- snapshot timing relative to the PPSV nightly backup; and
- the last successful restore-drill evidence.

## Nightly job

`ppsv-backup.timer` runs nightly at 02:15 Europe/Berlin with up to 15 minutes
of randomized delay and catches up after downtime. The default retention is 30
days.

The backup service:

- uses SQLite's backup mechanism rather than copying a live database file;
- writes to a partial file and moves it into place only after success;
- runs `PRAGMA integrity_check` on the result;
- creates a SHA-256 sidecar;
- copies the database backup to a disposable restore probe and opens it through
  the complete schema/integrity verifier;
- archives the fallback directory, verifies the archive can be listed, and
  compares it with the live fallback tree before creating its SHA-256 sidecar;
  and
- prunes database/fallback artifacts older than the configured retention.

Run and inspect it manually:

```bash
sudo systemctl start ppsv-backup.service
sudo systemctl status ppsv-backup.service --no-pager
sudo journalctl -u ppsv-backup.service -n 100 --no-pager
sudo systemctl list-timers ppsv-backup.timer
```

Do not treat a green timer as proof of recovery. Check that new non-empty
artifacts and sidecars exist on the expected external mount.

## Verify a backup without changing production

Choose a matching database and optional fallback archive from the same backup
window. With no `--apply`, the restore tool is read-only: it requires and checks
the SHA-256 sidecars, SQLite integrity/schema/foreign keys, archive readability,
and unsafe archive paths.

```bash
sudo /usr/local/libexec/ppsvf-app/restore_backup.sh \
  --database /external/ppsv/database/ppsv_projects_TIMESTAMP.sqlite \
  --fallback /external/ppsv/fallback/uploads_pending_pool_TIMESTAMP.tar.gz
```

Every artifact must have the one-record `.sha256` sidecar created by the backup
job. A missing, malformed, unsafe, or mismatched sidecar is a hard failure.

## Restore drill

At least after first installation and after material schema/storage changes,
perform an actual restore on a disposable VM or isolated restore environment:

1. Use the same reviewed application release and an isolated PPSV environment
   file whose database, fallback, pool, and public URL cannot touch production.
2. Verify the chosen backup with `restore_backup.sh` without `--apply`.
3. Apply it in the isolated target with both destructive-confirmation flags.
4. Start the application and run SQLite integrity and migration checks.
5. Open representative service and inquiry records, render their PDFs, inspect
   status history and mail attempts, and download representative files through
   the authorized path so checksums are exercised.
6. Restore a corresponding facility-pool snapshot into an isolated path and
   verify manifest counts and SHA-256 values.
7. Record artifact names/checksums, application revision, schema version,
   operator, duration, problems, and remediation.

Do not call backups production-ready until this drill succeeds.

## Applying a production restore

Applying a restore overwrites current database state and can discard every
request, status update, file record, and mail attempt created after the backup.
Obtain explicit incident authorization and identify the recovery point first.

The restore command requires both `--apply` and `--confirm-data-loss`:

```bash
sudo /usr/local/libexec/ppsvf-app/restore_backup.sh \
  --database /external/ppsv/database/ppsv_projects_TIMESTAMP.sqlite \
  --fallback /external/ppsv/fallback/uploads_pending_pool_TIMESTAMP.tar.gz \
  --apply \
  --confirm-data-loss
```

The script verifies inputs before stopping services, preserves a pre-restore
database/fallback copy under `/srv/ppsvf-app-data/pre_restore/TIMESTAMP`, stages
replacement state, rejects fallback symlinks, reapplies `2770`/`0660`
permissions, and restarts Shiny and the mail timer.

After it returns:

1. verify SQLite integrity and schema version;
2. select a code release compatible with that schema;
3. restore the primary pool to the same recovery point using the facility
   storage procedure;
4. verify pool/fallback files against database checksums;
5. run `scripts/verify_deployment.sh`;
6. exercise all three roles and a representative download/PDF; and
7. inspect the mail outbox before enabling or manually retrying delivery, so an
   old unsent row does not cause an unexpected duplicate.

Keep the pre-restore directory until the incident owner signs off. Any later
removal is an explicit operator retention action, not an application purge.

## Pool snapshots

The pool must be covered by the facility storage system; `backup.sh` does not
recursively archive it. The documented policy must answer:

- snapshot frequency and retention;
- whether open writes are crash-consistent;
- how a snapshot is mounted read-only for verification;
- how a single `PPSVnnnnnn` directory and a full pool are restored;
- who authorizes a restore; and
- how restored ownership, setgid mode, default ACL, and checksums are verified.

Align database/fallback backup time and pool snapshot time as closely as the
storage platform permits. On recovery, report any database file record that is
newer than the chosen pool snapshot rather than silently dropping it.

## Backup alerts and capacity

Monitor the systemd unit result, external mount availability, free space,
artifact age, and checksum verification. A locally created path at the expected
mount point is not evidence that external storage is mounted. If the mount
disappears, stop and restore it; do not let a local directory silently become
the backup destination.
